claim: Biogenic amines are recognized by GPCRs through an essential salt bridge between the ligand amino group and a highly conserved aspartic acid on the third transmembrane α-helix of the receptor (Asp3.32).
source: The biochemical and structural basis for biogenic amine recognition by GPCRs is well understood and involves an essential salt bridge between the ligand amino group and a highly conserved aspartic acid on the third transmembrane α-helix of the receptor (Asp3.32; Ballesteros-Weinstein indexing) (Katritch et al., 2013; Shi and Javitch, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Katritch et al., 2013; Shi and Javitch, 2002) describing the structural basis of amine recognition by GPCRs.

claim: Mutation of Asp3.32 in adrenaline, serotonin, acetylcholine, histamine, and dopamine receptors eliminates amine recognition.
source: Mutation of Asp3.32 in adrenaline, serotonin, acetylcholine, histamine, and dopamine receptors eliminates amine recognition (Shi and Javitch, 2002; Surgand et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to published mutagenesis studies (Shi and Javitch, 2002; Surgand et al., 2006).

source: There are 15 TAARs in mouse, 6 in human, and 112 in zebrafish

evidence: Supported by citations to published studies (Horowitz et al., 2014; Hussain et al., 2009; Liberles and Buck, 2006).

claim: Mouse TAAR5 detects the attractive and sexually dimorphic mouse odor trimethylamine.

source: A TAAR13c variant with a charge-neutralizing mutation at Asp5.42 has an altered ligand preference for monoamines rather than diamines.

source: Asp5.42 is retained in 84 out of 85 zebrafish TAARs that lack Asp3.32

evidence: Stated as findings from ligand identification experiments shown in Figures 3 and 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A large clade of olfactory GPCRs evolved a novel way to detect amines that involves a non-classical salt bridge to transmembrane α-helix V.

evidence: Proposed as a conclusion based on the ligand identification and mutagenesis data presented in the study.

claim: The TAAR13c homology model was based on the X-ray crystal structure of agonist-bound β2 adrenergic receptor (Protein Data Bank Entry 4LDE).
source: To gain structural insights into diamine recognition by the cadaverine receptor TAAR13c, we generated a TAAR13c homology model (Figure 1A) based on the X-ray crystal structure of agonist-bound β2 adrenergic receptor (Protein Data Bank Entry 4LDE) (Ring et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as the method used for structural modeling, with citation to the crystal structure (Ring et al., 2013).

claim: The β2 adrenergic receptor is the closest homolog (33% amino acid identity) of TAAR13c for which an active-state structure is currently available.
source: The β2 adrenergic receptor is the closest homolog (33% amino acid identity) of TAAR13c for which an active-state structure is currently available.
evidence: Stated as justification for the choice of template for homology modeling.

claim: Computational docking of cadaverine to TAAR13c positioned one cadaverine amino group near Asp1123.32 and the other near Asp2025.42.
source: Using the homology model, we performed computational docking of cadaverine to the orthosteric binding site. One cadaverine amino group of the docked ligand was located near Asp1123.32, which corresponds to the highly conserved amine-contact site in biogenic amine receptors. The other cadaverine amino group was positioned at the opposing end of the ligand-binding pocket, 3 Å away from another aspartate, Asp2025.42.
evidence: Stated as a result of computational docking studies using the homology model.

claim: Position 5.42 in several other GPCRs directly contacts ligands through hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, or van der Waals interactions.
source: Position 5.42 in several other GPCRs directly contacts ligands through hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, or van der Waals interactions (Surgand et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to published analysis of GPCR structures (Surgand et al., 2006).

claim: Charge-neutralizing mutation of Asp1123.32 in TAAR13c abrogates cadaverine responsiveness.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and described in the text.

claim: Charge-neutralizing mutation of Asp2025.42 in TAAR13c abrogates cadaverine responsiveness.
source: Charge-neutralizing mutation of D1123.32 and D2025.42 abrogates cadaverine responsiveness of zebrafish TAAR13c expressed in HEK-293 cells (mean ± sem, n = 3, **p<0.01 based on two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and described in the text.

claim: The TAAR13cD202A mutant is activated by the monoamine 3-methoxytyramine.

source: Thus, charge-neutralizing mutation of Asp5.42 transformed TAAR13c from a diamine receptor into a monoamine receptor.
